To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we found evidence for a recent population bottleneck associated with the European colonization, (2) we found that the bottleneck can account for much but not all of the reduction in genetic variation between the African and European populations, and (3) we found evidence of recent positive selection in several regions of the X chromosome, including the region containing the white locus.

1) the European population experienced a bottleneck about 3,000-16,000 ago; 2) the European population has less variation at some loci than expected given the bottleneck, suggesting that selection is responsible for some of this variation; and 3) the European population also has more variation at some locis than expected given the demographic history, suggesting that positive selection has acted to increase the frequency of some beneficial variants in the European population.

(1) a major population bottleneck occurred about 3-16 thousand years ago and that (2) the reduction in genetic variation observed in the derived European population is not explained entirely by this population bottleneck.

the identification of genomic regions in Drosophila that have been the target of positive selection.
the evolutionary forces acting on the X chromosome of Drosophila, with the aim of identifying regions that have been targets of positive selection in the recent evolutionary past.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have identified a number of regions of the genome where there is a deficiency in polymorphism that can be explained by selection.

the X chromosome of D. melanogaster has experienced a bottleneck of about 3,000 years ago, which can explain most of the variation reduction in this chromosome, and some of the variation reduction can be explained by the action of positive selection.

there is no evidence for selection on this chromosome in the European population, but there is evidence for selection in the African sample, which is not unexpected because the African population has not been exposed to the strong selective pressure that has been imposed on the European population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have detected evidence of selection on the X chromosome of D. melanogaster in both the ancestral African population and the derived European population.
we have identified a set of regions that may have experienced recent positive Darwinian selection.
we have detected evidence for both demography and positive selection on the Drosophia melanogaster X chromosome.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the bottleneck is not the main cause of the reduction in polymorphism in the European population, but rather that the bottleneck is just one of the factors that contribute to the reduction in polymorphisms.

we can identify genomic regions that have been targets of positive selection in a species by comparing patterns of DNA sequence variation in a population from the putative ancestral range with a derived population.
the X chromosome of the derived European population is enriched for regions that have been under positive selection.
